results.message: Your bishops covered for each other when one of them did real harm. Defend that.

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
We did not cover for a bishop who harmed someone. We kept the office itself from depending on the man who held it, so that what it gave did not vanish when he fell.

Augustine put the question plainly to a Donatist, through another man's voice. Someone had said to him: the traitor bishop who gave me baptism has condemned me. Augustine answered: “But He who is everywhere was there. He who is everywhere was there, the One in whose name I believed. You come from who knows where. No, you do not even come; you want me to come to you. You stay put here and tell me, ‘You were not baptized properly, because I was not there.’ Look at who was there.”

The One who gave it was there, and is everywhere.

This is the same conviction that traced the bishops' office back to the apostles by name. Augustine counted the line from Peter down to the present bishop of Rome, one name after another. Cyprian stated the principle underneath it: from Peter onward, the ordering of bishops through the changes of times and successions carries the Church itself forward.

What we refused to let a failed bishop's sin destroy was the validity of what he had given before he fell. We did not say his failure did not matter. We said it did not unmake the font or the ordination he had performed. Scripture itself stood above every bishop. A bishop's own letter could be corrected, and a council could be corrected by a later, greater one. But we would not let one man's failure destroy what belonged to the office he no longer deserved to hold.

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

sourced_by.citation: Augustine of Hippo, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, vol. VI

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258
